Neonates emerge weighing approximately 2.315 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.315 grams], a modest birth mass consistent with the altricial strategy typical of small-bodied cricetid rodents. Following parturition, the altricial neonates remain entirely dependent on maternal care for several weeks, during which they undergo rapid mass gain through exclusive milk ingestion. The body mass at weaning is a crucial determinant of subsequent juvenile survival, as individuals that achieve a higher mass at nutritional independence tend to exhibit greater overwinter survival rates and earlier onset of reproductive maturation in the following breeding season. This weaning mass of roughly 10.5 grams [Wwx = roughly 10.5 grams] is consistent with values reported for other temperate Peromyscus species of similar adult body size.

This fecundity level, combined with the capacity for rapid postpartum estrus, allows a single female to contribute substantial recruitment over the course of a single reproductive season. The combination of a relatively short gestation time and moderate litter size positions Peromyscus truei as a classic r-selected strategist among North American small mammals, capable of rapid population recovery following environmental perturbations.

Individuals that survive their first winter typically maintain high reproductive output for several consecutive seasons.
